title: Introduction to Media and Information Literacy
lesson:
Media and Information Literacy (MIL) refers to the ability to access, understand, analyze, evaluate, create, and communicate information through different forms of media. It helps people develop the skills needed to understand the information they encounter and make responsible decisions about how they use and share it.

In everyday life, people receive information from many sources, including television, radio, newspapers, books, websites, social media, online videos, podcasts, and other digital platforms. Because information is available almost everywhere, people need to know how to determine whether the information they encounter is accurate, relevant, reliable, and appropriate for its purpose.

For students, MIL is especially important because they regularly use information for school activities, research, discussions, and everyday communication. Students may encounter useful educational information, but they may also come across misleading posts, false claims, edited images, or unreliable sources. Developing media and information literacy helps students become more careful when receiving information and more responsible when creating or sharing content.
discussion:
Media refers to the different channels, platforms, or tools used to communicate information to an audience. Examples include television, radio, newspapers, magazines, websites, social media platforms, and online videos. Different forms of media may present information in different ways depending on their purpose and intended audience.

Information refers to facts, ideas, data, opinions, or knowledge that are communicated to people. Information can come from books, teachers, news reports, websites, social media posts, interviews, research studies, and other sources. However, the availability of information does not automatically mean that all information is accurate or trustworthy.

Media and Information Literacy helps people become careful users and creators of information. It involves asking questions such as: Who created the information? Where did it come from? What evidence supports the claim? Why was it created? Is the source reliable? These questions help individuals avoid accepting or sharing information without checking it first.

MIL also involves responsible communication. When creating or sharing information, people should consider whether their content is accurate, respectful, appropriate, and fair. Responsible media use also includes respecting other people's privacy, giving proper credit to sources, and avoiding the spread of harmful or misleading information.
example:
A student sees a post on social media claiming that classes are suspended because of bad weather. Instead of immediately believing or sharing the post, the student checks the official school page, verified announcements, or other reliable sources.

If the official announcement confirms the suspension, the student can confidently use the information. If no reliable source confirms the claim, the student avoids sharing it until the information can be verified.

This demonstrates media and information literacy because the student checks the source, evaluates the information, and makes a responsible decision before sharing it.
keyConcepts: Media provides different ways to communicate information.
Information includes facts, ideas, data, opinions, and knowledge.
Information can come from many different sources.
Not all information is accurate, reliable, or appropriate.
Information should be evaluated before being accepted or shared.
People can be both consumers and creators of media.
Responsible media use includes checking sources, respecting privacy, and giving proper credit.
MIL helps people make informed and responsible decisions.
keyTakeaway: Media and Information Literacy helps students become responsible users, evaluators, and creators of information. It teaches them to think carefully about where information comes from, whether it can be trusted, and how it should be used or shared.

title: Types of Media
lesson:
Media can take different forms depending on how information is created, presented, distributed, and accessed. People encounter media almost every day through printed materials, television, radio, websites, mobile applications, and social networking platforms.

The common types of media include print media, broadcast media, digital media, and social media. Each type has its own characteristics and methods of delivering information to an audience.

Print media includes newspapers, magazines, books, brochures, flyers, and other materials that are produced in printed form. Broadcast media includes television and radio, which distribute information and entertainment to audiences through audio or audiovisual programs. Digital media includes websites, online articles, digital books, videos, podcasts, and other content accessed through electronic devices. Social media includes online platforms where users can create, post, share, comment on, and interact with content.

Understanding the different types of media helps students recognize how information reaches audiences and how the characteristics of a medium can affect the way information is presented.
discussion:
Print Media presents information through physical or printed materials. Newspapers and magazines, for example, often contain news articles, features, advertisements, and other written content. Books and brochures may be used for educational, informational, or promotional purposes.

Broadcast Media communicates information through television and radio. Television can combine spoken words, images, videos, and sounds, while radio mainly relies on spoken words, music, and sound. Broadcast media can reach large audiences and is commonly used for news, entertainment, education, and public announcements.

Digital Media refers to content that is created, stored, and accessed using digital devices. Examples include websites, online news articles, e-books, educational videos, podcasts, and mobile applications. Digital media allows information to be accessed quickly and can make it easier for users to search, save, and share content.

Social Media allows users to communicate and interact with one another while creating and sharing content. Examples include social networking, video-sharing, and messaging platforms. Unlike traditional forms of media, social media users can often participate directly by posting their own content, commenting, reacting, and sharing information.

Different types of media can also be combined. For example, a news organization may publish a story in a newspaper, upload the same story to its website, discuss it on television, and share it through social media. Although the topic may be the same, the information can be presented differently depending on the medium and its intended audience.
example:
A news event may be reported through several types of media. A newspaper may provide a detailed written article, while television may show video footage and interviews. A news website may provide written information together with photographs, videos, and links to related stories. On social media, users may share the news, comment on it, or discuss their opinions.

Although all of these forms may discuss the same event, the amount of information, presentation style, and level of interaction may differ. This is why students should consider the type of media they are using when receiving and evaluating information.
keyConcepts: Print media includes newspapers, books, magazines, brochures, and other printed materials.
Broadcast media includes television and radio.
Digital media includes websites, online articles, videos, podcasts, and digital publications.
Social media allows users to create, share, and interact with content.
Different types of media have different ways of presenting information.
The same topic may appear differently across different media platforms.
Media can serve education, news, communication, entertainment, and other purposes.
Understanding media types helps users better understand how information is delivered.
keyTakeaway: Understanding different types of media helps students recognize how information is created, presented, distributed, and shared. By knowing the characteristics of each medium, students can better understand and evaluate the information they encounter in their everyday lives.

title: Information Sources and Credibility
lesson:
Information sources are materials, people, organizations, or platforms from which information is obtained. Students use different sources every day when studying, doing research, completing school activities, or simply looking for answers to questions.

Examples of information sources include books, academic journals, newspapers, government websites, interviews, educational websites, news organizations, online databases, and social media posts. Some sources are created by experts or established organizations, while others may be created by individuals with different levels of knowledge or experience.

Not every source has the same level of credibility. Credibility refers to how trustworthy, reliable, and believable a source is. A source may contain useful information, but students should still examine where the information came from and whether it is supported by evidence.

When using information for academic work, students should evaluate the source before accepting its claims. Checking the author, publication date, evidence, publisher, and purpose can help determine whether the information is appropriate for a particular task.
discussion:
A credible source provides information that can be supported by evidence and comes from a trustworthy, knowledgeable, or qualified source. Credibility does not simply depend on how professional a website looks or how many people have shared a post. Students should examine the actual source and the information it provides.

The author is important because the creator of the information may have relevant knowledge, education, training, or experience related to the topic. Knowing who wrote or produced the information can help readers determine whether the source is appropriate.

The publication date is also important. Some information changes over time, especially in areas such as laws, technology, statistics, health, and current events. A source that is outdated may no longer accurately represent the current situation.

Students should also look for evidence. Reliable information is often supported by data, research, references, documents, quotations from experts, or other verifiable evidence. Claims without supporting evidence should be examined carefully.

The publisher can also provide useful information about a source. Government agencies, universities, academic publishers, established news organizations, and recognized institutions may provide information for specific purposes. However, students should still evaluate the actual content instead of assuming that every source from an organization is automatically correct.

Finally, students should consider the purpose of the source. Information may be created to educate, inform, entertain, advertise, persuade, or influence an audience. Understanding the purpose helps students recognize possible biases or limitations in the information.

When possible, students should also compare information from multiple reliable sources. If several trustworthy sources provide consistent information, this can provide stronger support for understanding a topic.
example:
A student is researching information about Philippine laws and finds two sources. The first is an anonymous social media post that provides a short explanation but does not identify its author or provide supporting references. The second is an official government website that provides information about the law and identifies the government agency responsible for the information.

Instead of immediately using the social media post, the student checks the official government source and compares the information. The student uses the more appropriate source for the research and verifies important details before including them.

This demonstrates responsible information use because the student checks the source, considers its credibility, and verifies the information before using it.
keyConcepts: Author – Who created the information, and do they have relevant knowledge or qualifications?
Date – When was the information published or last updated?
Evidence – Are the claims supported by research, data, references, or other reliable evidence?
Purpose – Why was the information created? Is it intended to inform, educate, persuade, entertain, or advertise?
Publisher – Who published or distributed the information?
Accuracy – Can the information be checked against other reliable sources?
Relevance – Is the information appropriate and useful for the topic or task?
Source Comparison – Do other reliable sources support the same information?
keyTakeaway: Students should evaluate the credibility, accuracy, relevance, and purpose of information sources before using or sharing information. By checking the author, date, evidence, publisher, and purpose, students can make more informed decisions about which sources are appropriate for academic work and everyday use.

title: Evaluating Information
lesson:
Evaluating information means examining information carefully before deciding whether it is useful, accurate, reliable, and appropriate for a particular purpose. With the large amount of information available through websites, social media, news platforms, books, and other sources, students need to develop the ability to determine which information can be trusted and used.

Information may look convincing even when it contains incomplete, outdated, or incorrect claims. A professional-looking website, a large number of views, or many social media shares does not automatically mean that the information is accurate. Students should look beyond the appearance or popularity of information and examine the source and evidence behind it.

Students can use five important factors when evaluating information: currency, relevance, authority, accuracy, and purpose. These factors help students decide whether a source is suitable for academic research, school activities, or everyday decision-making.
discussion:
Currency refers to how recent the information is. Some topics change quickly, so students should check when the information was published or last updated. For example, information about technology, laws, current events, or statistics may become outdated over time. However, older sources may still be useful for historical topics when their publication date is appropriate for the purpose.

Relevance refers to how closely the information relates to the topic or question being studied. A source may be reliable but still not be useful if it does not directly address the student's research topic. Students should determine whether the information provides the details they actually need.

Authority refers to the qualifications, expertise, or credibility of the person, organization, or institution responsible for the information. Students should consider who created the content and whether the creator has appropriate knowledge or experience related to the topic.

Accuracy refers to whether the information is correct and supported by evidence. Students should look for references, research findings, data, official records, or other evidence that can support the claims. Comparing information with other reliable sources can also help identify errors or inconsistencies.

Purpose refers to the reason why the information was created. A source may be intended to inform, educate, entertain, advertise, or persuade an audience. Understanding the purpose can help students recognize whether the information may contain opinions, promotional content, or a particular point of view.

These five factors should be considered together. A source may be recent but lack evidence, or it may come from an authoritative organization but be irrelevant to the student's topic. Evaluating information requires looking at the source as a whole rather than relying on only one factor.
example:
A student is researching a recent scientific discovery and finds an article published several years before the discovery was made. Even if the website appears professional, the student should question whether the article can provide accurate information about the recent discovery.

The student then looks for newer sources from universities, scientific organizations, or research publications. The student compares the information and checks whether the claims are supported by evidence.

This demonstrates information evaluation because the student considers the currency, relevance, authority, and accuracy of the sources before using them.
keyConcepts: Check Currency – Determine when the information was published or last updated.
Check Relevance – Determine whether the information directly relates to the topic or purpose.
Check Authority – Consider the qualifications or credibility of the author or organization.
Check Accuracy – Look for evidence and compare important claims with reliable sources.
Check Purpose – Identify why the information was created and who the intended audience is.
Avoid judging information based only on its popularity, appearance, or number of shares.
Compare important information with other reliable sources when possible.
keyTakeaway: Evaluating information helps students distinguish useful and reliable information from information that may be inaccurate, outdated, irrelevant, or unsuitable. By checking its currency, relevance, authority, accuracy, and purpose, students can make more informed decisions about the information they use, believe, and share.

title: Misinformation and Disinformation
lesson:
Information shared online is not always accurate or complete. People can encounter false claims, misleading posts, edited images, manipulated videos, or incorrect information through social media, websites, messaging applications, and other platforms. Because information can be shared quickly, false information may reach many people before it can be checked.

Misinformation refers to false or inaccurate information that is shared without necessarily intending to deceive others. A person may share misinformation because they believe the information is true, misunderstood the original content, or did not check the source first.

Disinformation, on the other hand, refers to false or misleading information that is deliberately created or shared with the intention of deceiving or misleading people. It may be created to influence opinions, cause confusion, attract attention, or achieve another purpose.

Both misinformation and disinformation can affect how people understand events and make decisions. This is why students should develop the habit of checking information before believing or sharing it.
discussion:
False or misleading information can appear in different forms. Some examples include fabricated stories, misleading headlines, edited photographs, manipulated videos, fake quotes, false statistics, and statements taken out of context.

A misleading headline may make a story sound more extreme than the actual information in the article. An edited image may also create a false impression about an event. Similarly, an old photograph or video may be presented as if it were related to a recent event.

Social media and messaging platforms can contribute to the rapid spread of false information because users can easily repost, share, or forward content to other people. A claim may be shared many times even when its original source is unclear.

Students can reduce the spread of false information by practicing verification. Before sharing a claim, they can check the original source, examine the date, look for supporting evidence, compare the information with other reliable sources, and determine whether reputable organizations or institutions have reported the same information.

Students should also be careful with information that creates a strong emotional reaction. Content that is designed to make people immediately angry, afraid, or excited may encourage quick sharing before the information has been properly checked.

Being responsible with information does not mean that students must know whether every claim is true immediately. When information cannot be verified, it is better to pause and avoid sharing it until reliable evidence is available.
example:
A student receives a message in a group chat claiming that classes will be suspended the following day because of bad weather. The message does not provide a reliable source and asks students to forward it to their classmates.

Instead of immediately forwarding the message, the student checks the school's official announcement page and other reliable sources. The student discovers that there is no official announcement confirming the suspension.

The student decides not to share the unverified message. This demonstrates responsible information use because the student checks the source and verifies the claim before sharing it.
keyConcepts: Misinformation is false or inaccurate information shared without necessarily intending to deceive.
Disinformation is false or misleading information deliberately created or shared to deceive others.
False information can appear as fake stories, misleading headlines, edited images, manipulated videos, fake quotes, or claims taken out of context.
Social media and messaging platforms can allow information to spread quickly.
A large number of views, likes, or shares does not automatically make information true.
Information should be checked against reliable sources before being shared.
Students should examine the original source, date, evidence, and context of a claim.
When information cannot be verified, it is safer to avoid sharing it.
keyTakeaway: Think, check, and verify before believing or sharing information. Understanding the difference between misinformation and disinformation helps students become more responsible users of media and avoid contributing to the spread of false or misleading information.

title: Responsible Use of Social Media and Digital Citizenship
lesson:
Social media allows people to communicate, share information, create content, and interact with others. Platforms can be useful for education, entertainment, collaboration, news, and staying connected with friends, classmates, and communities. However, because users can easily publish and share content, responsible behavior is important when using digital platforms.

Digital citizenship refers to responsible, respectful, and appropriate behavior when using digital technologies and participating in online communities. It involves understanding how online actions can affect oneself and others.

Being a responsible digital citizen includes respecting other people, protecting personal information, thinking carefully before posting, communicating appropriately, and following platform rules and community standards. Students should also understand that information shared online can sometimes reach a much larger audience than originally intended.
discussion:
One important part of digital citizenship is understanding the digital footprint. A digital footprint refers to the information and traces a person leaves through their online activities. This may include posts, comments, photos, videos, likes, searches, shared content, and other interactions.

Some parts of a digital footprint may remain accessible even after content is deleted from a platform. Other people may have already viewed, downloaded, copied, or shared the content. Because of this, students should think carefully about the possible consequences of posting something before making it public.

Privacy is another important part of responsible social media use. Personal information such as a full name, address, phone number, passwords, school details, or private photographs should be handled carefully. Students should avoid sharing sensitive information publicly or with people they do not know.

Digital citizens should also respect the privacy and consent of others. A person may not want their photograph, personal information, or private conversation shared online. Asking for permission before posting content involving other people helps respect their choices and boundaries.

Responsible communication is also important. Online conversations should remain respectful even when people have different opinions. Students should avoid harassment, offensive comments, unnecessary arguments, and sharing content intended to embarrass or harm another person.

Before posting or sharing something, students can ask themselves: Is it accurate? Is it respectful? Is it appropriate? Does it reveal private information? Would I be comfortable if other people saw it? These questions can help users make more thoughtful decisions online.
example:
A student wants to upload a photo of classmates during a school activity. Before posting it, the student asks whether the classmates are comfortable with the photo being shared.

One classmate does not want the photo posted publicly. The student respects the classmate's decision and chooses not to upload the photo.

This demonstrates responsible digital citizenship because the student respects privacy, asks for consent, and considers how online actions may affect others.
keyConcepts: Social media allows people to communicate, create, and share content.
Digital citizenship involves responsible and respectful behavior when using technology.
A digital footprint is the information and traces a person leaves through online activities.
Users should protect their personal and private information.
Other people's privacy and consent should be respected.
Students should think carefully before posting, commenting, or sharing content.
Online communication should remain respectful and appropriate.
Following platform rules and community standards is part of responsible digital behavior.
Content shared online may be copied, saved, or redistributed by others.
keyTakeaway: Responsible digital citizenship means using technology respectfully, safely, and thoughtfully. By protecting personal information, respecting privacy and consent, communicating appropriately, and thinking before posting, students can contribute to a safer and more respectful online environment.

title: Media Bias and Objectivity
lesson:
Media can present information from different perspectives. The same event or issue may be reported in different ways depending on the information selected, the sources used, the language chosen, and the details emphasized.

Media bias refers to a tendency in the selection or presentation of information that may favor a particular perspective, viewpoint, or interpretation. Bias does not always mean that the information is completely false. Instead, it may influence which parts of a topic receive more attention and how audiences understand the issue.

Objectivity generally refers to presenting information fairly and based on relevant evidence rather than personal preference. In practice, completely eliminating perspective from media can be difficult because decisions about what information to include, emphasize, or leave out can influence how a story is understood.

Because of this, students should learn to recognize possible bias and examine information carefully instead of immediately accepting one presentation as the complete picture.
discussion:
Media bias can appear in different ways. Word choice can influence how an audience feels about a person, event, or issue. For example, two reports may describe the same action using words with different emotional meanings.

Headlines can also affect interpretation. A headline may emphasize one part of an event while leaving out other details. Since many people read only headlines or short summaries, the wording can strongly influence their first impression.

Images and videos can also shape how information is understood. The choice of photograph, video clip, or visual angle may highlight certain aspects of an event while other aspects receive less attention.

Students should also examine the sources and evidence used in a report. A report that includes information from several relevant and credible sources may provide more context than one that relies heavily on a single source. However, students should still examine what each source actually says and whether the evidence supports the claims being made.

Another way to recognize possible bias is to consider what information may have been included or omitted. Leaving out relevant context can affect how audiences interpret an event, even when the information that is presented is technically accurate.

Comparing multiple credible sources can help students identify differences in wording, evidence, emphasis, and perspective. The goal is not simply to choose one source immediately, but to examine the available information and develop a more informed understanding of the topic.
example:
Two news reports describe the same public event but use different headlines and emphasize different details. One report focuses on the actions of the organizers, while the other focuses on the reactions of participants.

A student reads both reports, examines the sources and evidence they provide, and checks additional credible sources for context. Instead of relying on only one report, the student considers how the different presentations may affect the understanding of the event.

This demonstrates responsible media literacy because the student recognizes different perspectives, examines evidence, and compares sources before forming an understanding of the topic.
keyConcepts: Media can present information from different perspectives.
Media bias can influence how information is selected or presented.
Bias does not necessarily mean that every part of a report is false.
Objectivity involves presenting information fairly and based on relevant evidence.
Word choice can influence how audiences interpret information.
Headlines can emphasize particular details or perspectives.
Images and videos can influence how an event is perceived.
Sources and supporting evidence should be examined carefully.
Information that is included or omitted can affect interpretation.
Comparing multiple credible sources can provide broader context.
keyTakeaway: Understanding media perspectives and possible bias helps students evaluate information more carefully. By examining word choice, headlines, images, sources, evidence, and different presentations of the same topic, students can develop a more informed understanding of the information they encounter.

title: Information Ethics and Responsible Information Use
lesson:
Information ethics refers to the principles and responsibilities involved in the responsible use, creation, sharing, and management of information. It involves respecting people's privacy, intellectual property, authorship, and rights when accessing or using information.

Students regularly use information from books, websites, academic articles, videos, social media, interviews, and other sources. This information can be useful for learning and completing school activities, but it should be used responsibly and honestly.

Responsible information use means acknowledging the sources of information, avoiding plagiarism, protecting private information, respecting creators' work, and carefully considering the possible effects of sharing information. Students should also avoid intentionally spreading harmful, misleading, or false content.

Information ethics applies not only to academic work but also to everyday online activities. The way a person collects, uses, stores, and shares information can affect other people. Understanding information ethics helps students make decisions that respect both the value of information and the rights of the people connected to it.
discussion:
Ethical information use is important in both academic and everyday settings. In academic work, students often use ideas, facts, quotations, images, or other materials created by other people. When using these materials, students should properly acknowledge the original source instead of presenting someone else's work or ideas as their own.

Plagiarism is one example of unethical information use. It occurs when a person uses another person's words, ideas, or work without giving appropriate credit. Students can avoid plagiarism by using proper citations, quotation marks when directly quoting, and appropriate paraphrasing while acknowledging the original source.

Another important principle is respect for intellectual property. Creators may have rights over their original writings, photographs, videos, artwork, music, software, and other forms of creative work. Students should not automatically assume that anything available online can be copied, modified, or redistributed without restrictions.

Privacy is also an important part of responsible information use. Personal information may include names, addresses, contact details, photographs, private conversations, school information, or other information that a person may not want publicly shared. Students should avoid sharing another person's private information without appropriate permission.

Students should also consider the purpose and possible consequences of sharing information. Even information that is technically true may be inappropriate to share if it exposes someone's private information or causes unnecessary harm. Responsible users should think about who may see the information and how it could affect others.

When creating or sharing information, students should also aim to be honest and accurate. They should avoid changing information in a way that creates a misleading impression and should correct mistakes when they discover them.
example:
A student is preparing a school report and finds useful information in an online article. The student includes some of the article's ideas in the report and provides the appropriate source instead of presenting those ideas as their own.

The student also uses quotation marks for any exact words taken from the article and identifies the source. This demonstrates ethical information use because the student acknowledges the creator and distinguishes the source's ideas from their own work.
keyConcepts: Information should be used responsibly, honestly, and carefully.
Sources should be properly acknowledged when their information or ideas are used.
Plagiarism should be avoided by giving appropriate credit to original creators.
Intellectual property refers to rights connected to original creations and works.
Personal and private information should be protected.
Other people's information should not be shared without appropriate permission.
Creators' rights and authorship should be respected.
Information should not be intentionally changed or presented in a misleading way.
Students should consider the possible effects of sharing information.
Ethical information use applies to both academic activities and everyday digital communication.
keyTakeaway: Responsible information use requires honesty, respect for other people's rights, and careful handling of information. By acknowledging sources, avoiding plagiarism, protecting privacy, respecting creators, and considering the consequences of sharing information, students can become more ethical and responsible users and creators of information.

title: Copyright, Plagiarism, and Proper Attribution
lesson:
Copyright is a form of legal protection for original creative works. It can apply to works such as books, photographs, music, videos, artwork, written materials, software, and other original creative content. Copyright generally gives creators certain rights over how their works are used, reproduced, distributed, or shared, subject to applicable laws and exceptions.

Because so much creative content is available online, students may easily encounter materials that can be useful for school activities. However, being able to access or view something online does not automatically mean that it can be copied, modified, or redistributed without restrictions. Students should pay attention to the permissions, licenses, or rules that apply to the material they want to use.

Plagiarism occurs when a person presents another person's words, ideas, or work as their own without appropriate acknowledgment. It can happen when students copy text directly, use another person's ideas without citation, or submit someone else's work as if they created it themselves.

Proper attribution means giving appropriate credit to the original creator or source when using their work or ideas. Attribution allows readers to identify where the information came from and recognizes the contribution of the original creator.
discussion:
Students may use information and creative materials for academic purposes, but they should follow appropriate rules for citation, attribution, copyright, and permitted use. The specific requirements may depend on the type of material, how it is being used, and the applicable rules or license.

One common form of plagiarism is direct copying. This happens when a student copies words from a source and presents them as their own without quotation marks and proper citation. When exact words are necessary, students should identify the borrowed text and provide the appropriate citation.

Another form is using someone else's ideas or information without acknowledgment. Even when the exact wording is changed, the original idea may still belong to another source. Students should therefore cite sources when required by the academic citation style they are using.

Paraphrasing means expressing information from a source using one's own words and sentence structure. However, paraphrasing does not automatically remove the need to acknowledge the source. The information or idea still came from the original creator, so the source should be credited when citation is required.

Students should also understand the difference between copyright and plagiarism. Copyright is a legal protection related to the rights of creators and the use of their original works. Plagiarism is an issue of academic and ethical integrity involving the failure to properly acknowledge another person's work or ideas. A work can have copyright considerations even when it is properly attributed, and attribution alone does not necessarily mean that every use is permitted.

Proper attribution also helps readers verify information and locate the original source. In research and academic writing, citations and references make it easier for readers to check the evidence behind a student's work.
example:
A student finds a useful paragraph from an online article while preparing a research paper. Instead of copying the paragraph directly and presenting it as their own, the student rewrites the information using their own words and sentence structure.

The student still identifies and cites the original source because the idea came from that article. If the student wants to use the exact words from the paragraph, they use appropriate quotation and citation practices.

This demonstrates responsible academic practice because the student acknowledges the original source and clearly distinguishes borrowed information from their own ideas.
keyConcepts: Copyright provides legal protection for many original creative works.
Copyright may apply to books, photographs, music, videos, artwork, software, and other creative content.
Accessing content online does not automatically mean that it can be freely copied or redistributed.
Plagiarism involves presenting another person's words, ideas, or work as one's own without appropriate acknowledgment.
Attribution gives credit to the original creator or source.
Direct quotations should be properly identified and cited.
Paraphrased information may still require citation because the original idea came from another source.
Copyright and plagiarism are related to responsible information use but refer to different concerns.
Students should follow appropriate academic citation and attribution practices.
Proper attribution helps readers identify and verify the original source.
keyTakeaway: Giving proper credit to creators and sources promotes academic honesty and responsible information use. By understanding copyright, avoiding plagiarism, properly attributing sources, and following appropriate citation practices, students can use information and creative materials respectfully and responsibly.

title: Advertising and Persuasive Media
lesson:
Advertising is a form of communication designed to promote products, services, ideas, or organizations. Advertisements can appear in many forms of media, including television, radio, websites, social media, posters, newspapers, mobile applications, online videos, and streaming platforms.

Advertising is commonly created to attract an audience's attention and encourage people to take a particular action, such as buying a product, trying a service, visiting a website, supporting an idea, or remembering a brand.

Advertisements often use persuasive techniques to influence how audiences think, feel, or behave. These techniques may include emotional appeals, testimonials, repetition, attractive visuals, celebrity or influencer endorsements, special offers, slogans, and claims about a product or service.

Because advertisements are designed to persuade, students should understand that their main purpose is not always to provide complete or neutral information. An advertisement may highlight the benefits of a product while providing less attention to limitations, conditions, or information that may make the product less appealing.
discussion:
Understanding persuasive techniques helps students recognize how advertisements attempt to influence audiences.

An emotional appeal uses feelings such as happiness, excitement, fear, confidence, or belonging to encourage audiences to respond to an advertisement. For example, an advertisement may show people becoming happier or more successful after using a particular product.

A testimonial uses statements or experiences from customers, celebrities, influencers, professionals, or other individuals to promote a product or service. Testimonials can make an advertisement appear more trustworthy, but students should still consider whether the person's experience provides enough evidence to support the advertising claim.

Repetition involves repeatedly presenting a brand name, slogan, message, or product feature so that it becomes easier for audiences to remember. Repeated exposure can make a message familiar even when familiarity does not necessarily prove that the claim is true.

Attractive visuals may include colorful designs, appealing photographs, video effects, or carefully selected images. These elements can capture attention and influence how audiences feel about a product.

Advertisements may also use special offers, such as discounts, limited-time deals, free items, or bundled products. These offers can encourage audiences to make quick decisions. Students should check the conditions of an offer instead of relying only on the promotional message.

Another important technique is the use of claims. Advertisements may describe a product as "the best," "the most effective," "number one," or "recommended by experts." Such statements should be examined carefully because some claims may require evidence, qualifications, or additional context.

Students should learn to distinguish factual information from persuasive language. A statement such as a product's price can usually be checked directly, while a statement claiming that the product is "the best" may involve an opinion or a claim that requires supporting evidence.
example:
An advertisement states that a particular product is "the number one choice" and shows several happy customers using it. The advertisement also uses attractive images and an emotional message about improving people's lives.

Instead of immediately accepting the claim, a media-literate student asks what "number one choice" means and whether the statement is supported by reliable evidence. The student checks whether the advertisement provides information about how the claim was determined and considers whether other relevant information has been left out.

This demonstrates media literacy because the student recognizes the persuasive techniques and evaluates the advertising claims instead of accepting them immediately.
keyConcepts: Advertising promotes products, services, ideas, or organizations.
Advertisements can appear across many types of media.
Advertising uses persuasive techniques to influence audiences.
Emotional appeals use feelings to encourage a particular response.
Testimonials use statements or experiences from individuals to build interest or trust.
Repetition makes messages, slogans, or brand names more familiar.
Attractive visuals can capture attention and influence audience perception.
Special offers can encourage audiences to act quickly.
Advertising claims should be checked for evidence and context.
Students should distinguish factual information from persuasive language.
Advertisements may emphasize benefits while giving less attention to limitations or conditions.
keyTakeaway: Media literacy helps students recognize persuasive techniques and evaluate advertising claims carefully. By identifying emotional appeals, testimonials, repetition, visuals, special offers, and unsupported claims, students can make more informed decisions instead of accepting advertising messages without question.
